worldSentence: Military risk returned faster than diplomacy could contain it: the United States struck Iranian launchers at Hormuz, Iran answered against U.S. bases in Jordan, and oil moved back above $90 while Washington prepared another layer of financial pressure.
standfirst: The first known U.S. strikes on Iran since late July interrupted the shift toward sanctions and mediation, though the immediate Iranian response caused no reported significant damage. Beyond the Gulf, Iceland rejected renewed EU talks, China's factories improved without escaping contraction, and Washington said future Venezuelan barrels would refill an emergency reserve now near a 44-year low. Malaysia converted high energy costs into household relief and mass AI access, while Qatar extended its national card scheme into Samsung Wallet.

connected.title: Governments are trying to convert exposure into control.

signals.label: BRENT
signals.text: Crude crossed the threshold after the first U.S. strike on Iran in weeks.

signals.label: CHINA PMI
signals.text: Manufacturing improved, but the broader economy still failed to expand.

signals.label: ICELAND NO
signals.text: Voters rejected reopening EU accession talks despite security pressure.

connected.note: The overnight stories are different versions of the same governing problem. Washington is using force, sanctions and Venezuelan oil rights to reduce exposure to Iran; Iceland chose policy control over a deeper European option; Malaysia used subsidies and digital access to cushion imported shocks; Qatar is localising payment rails. Each intervention creates leverage, but each also depends on execution that the announcement itself cannot prove.

stories.sourceNote: U.S. official, Iranian media + Reuters/AP · overnight
stories.title: The U.S. struck Iran again—and Tehran answered against American bases in Jordan.
stories.changed: U.S. forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, the first known American strikes on Iran since late July. A U.S. official said Revolutionary Guards units were preparing rockets fitted with sea mines. Iranian media said Tehran retaliated against two U.S. bases in Jordan with missiles and drones; a U.S.-sourced report said nearly all incoming weapons were intercepted and no significant impact had been reported. Brent crude rose more than 2% and crossed $90 a barrel in early Asian trade.
stories.matters: The exchange breaks a period in which Washington had emphasised blockade and financial pressure while Qatar and Oman tried to create a maritime off-ramp. Larak sits inside the strait, so a tactical strike on launchers is also a contest over who sets the terms of passage. The limited initial damage does not make the episode minor: repeated action and retaliation can close diplomatic room, raise insurance and freight costs, and expose Qatar and other hosts of U.S. forces to renewed regional spillover.
stories.watch: Whether either side treats the exchange as complete; verified casualty or damage reports in Jordan; new mining or shipping incidents around Hormuz; U.S. force-protection changes across the Gulf; Qatar and Oman's mediation contacts; Brent, tanker traffic and war-risk insurance; and the unnamed bank Washington says it will sanction this week.

group.label: The lead
group.title: A contained exchange can still reset the bargaining environment.
group.note: The strikes and response are confirmed by official or attributed reporting; motive, launcher readiness and the absence of damage still rely on the parties' accounts.

background.title: Force and financial isolation are now operating on the same clock
background.text: The United States had spent recent weeks describing a pivot toward sanctions and a maritime blockade, while Iran acknowledged steep trade and inflation damage but kept control of Hormuz as bargaining leverage. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said another bank would be sanctioned this week and that he would press G20 counterparts—including China—over dealings with Iran. The Larak strike shows that economic pressure has not displaced military action. It now sits beside it, making it harder for mediators to establish whether a shipping arrangement would pause attacks or merely narrow their targets.
background.known: The U.S. confirmed striking two launchers; Iran announced retaliation; oil rose; Bessent confirmed a planned bank sanction without naming the institution.
background.new: Direct U.S.–Iran fire resumed after more than a month, linking the physical contest inside Hormuz to the financial campaign opening at the G20.

left.label: Confirmed escalation
left.text: U.S. action on Iranian territory was followed by an Iranian-claimed attack on U.S. bases in Jordan.

right.label: Damage still provisional
right.text: No significant impact was initially reported, and independent verification of targets and interceptions remains limited.

sources.label: Reuters · Larak strike and Iranian response
AP · next U.S. bank sanction and G20 pressure

stories.sourceNote: National Electoral Commission + AP · final result
stories.title: Iceland rejected renewed EU accession talks by 52.8% to 47.2%.
stories.changed: The final result reversed the narrow early lead carried in yesterday's edition. More than 82% of eligible voters participated, and Reykjavík was the only region with a majority for reopening talks. Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said the government would respect the result and would not return the question to the top of its agenda unless something major changes.
stories.matters: The vote closes, for now, the fastest plausible route for adding a wealthy Arctic state to the European Union. Security anxiety after U.S. pressure on Greenland was not enough to outweigh control of fisheries, the króna and independent trade policy. Iceland remains inside the European Economic Area and Schengen, preserving much of its economic integration without accepting the institutional terms of membership.
stories.watch: Whether the close result strains the governing coalition; how Iceland manages defence and Arctic coordination outside the EU; future U.S. pressure around Greenland; fisheries negotiations with Europe; and whether a material security or currency shock reopens the question before the government's stated two-year horizon.

group.label: The world beyond the lead
group.title: The early count became a clear no.
group.note: This is a final electoral result, not a projection; it rejected negotiations rather than voting directly on membership.

background.title: Iceland chose its existing halfway house
background.text: Iceland already applies many EU single-market rules through the EEA and participates in passport-free Schengen travel, but retains national control over fishing waters and its currency. Supporters of talks wanted to test whether membership and eventually the euro could improve security and financing conditions. Opponents argued that the present arrangement captures most commercial benefits while keeping critical sovereignty. Because any negotiated accession deal would have required a second referendum, the ballot was principally a vote on whether to expand the option set. Voters declined even that step.
background.known: The National Electoral Commission reported the margin; the government pledged to respect it; turnout exceeded 82%.
background.new: The completed geographic count eliminated the early yes lead and showed support concentrated in the capital.

right.label: Europe link remains
right.text: The result does not remove Iceland from the EEA, Schengen or NATO.

sources.label: AP · final result and political response

stories.sourceNote: National Bureau of Statistics + Reuters · Monday
stories.title: China's factories improved to 49.8, but services and construction kept the whole economy in contraction.
stories.changed: China's official manufacturing PMI rose from 49.2 in July to 49.8 in August, beating the 49.6 consensus but remaining below the 50 expansion line for a second month. Manufacturing output reached 50.4 and new orders 50.6, while employment stayed at 48.7. Non-manufacturing activity was flat at 49.0 and the composite output index reached only 49.5.
stories.matters: The data resist both collapse and rebound narratives. Electronics and high-tech manufacturing are expanding, but services, construction, smaller firms and employment remain weak. That mix reinforces China's reliance on industrial capacity and external demand precisely as Washington asks G20 members to raise trade barriers and force a shift toward domestic consumption.
stories.watch: Private-sector PMIs this week; property and construction activity; consumer and services demand; employment; September fiscal or credit support; the G20 response to U.S. calls for coordinated trade barriers; and whether new export orders remain above 50 after the temporary improvement.

group.label: Economy & markets
group.title: Better manufacturing did not produce broad expansion.
group.note: A PMI below 50 still signals contraction; the important detail is where momentum returned and where it did not.

background.title: The composition matters more than the headline beat
background.text: Large manufacturers moved back into expansion at 50.6, while medium and small firms remained below 50. High-technology manufacturing reached 52.9 and equipment manufacturing 51.4, but consumer-goods producers were at 49.0 and energy-intensive industry at 47.9. New export orders edged to 50.1 even as imports remained at 48.6. This is consistent with a state-supported production machine finding pockets of demand while households, services and labour absorb less of the recovery. It can sustain output, but it also intensifies the trade imbalance confronting the G20.
background.known: The official survey covered 3,200 manufacturing and 4,300 non-manufacturing firms and showed the main output, demand and employment sub-indexes.
background.new: Orders and production returned to expansion, but the composite index remained below 50 because weakness broadened outside advanced manufacturing.

left.label: Real improvement
left.text: Manufacturing rose 0.6 points; output and new orders both crossed 50.

right.label: Not a rebound
right.text: The composite was 49.5, non-manufacturing 49.0 and small firms 47.9.

stories.title: Washington says Venezuelan oil will refill an emergency reserve near a 44-year low.
stories.changed: President Donald Trump said oil from the new U.S.–Venezuela agreement would begin replenishing the Strategic Petroleum Reserve shortly. The stockpile held about 290 million barrels on 21 August, close to its lowest level in 44 years after repeated drawdowns. The wider deal claims majority U.S. control over fields containing more than 65 billion barrels, but no public contract specifies the ownership vehicle, delivery schedule, investment burden or enforceable rights.
stories.matters: This turns the Venezuela agreement from a claim on distant underground reserves into a stated near-term energy-security plan. The gap between the two is large. Venezuela's heavy-oil industry requires capital, equipment and stable operating rules before output can rise materially, while an emergency reserve needs deliverable barrels and procurement terms. The announcement signals strategic intent; it does not yet create physical inventory.
stories.watch: A published contract; the private operator and financing structure; actual cargo nominations to U.S. reserve sites; crude quality and refinery logistics; Treasury sanctions licences; Venezuelan production and export data; the treatment of existing creditors and partners; and whether Congress challenges the arrangement.

group.label: Energy & capital allocation
group.title: Reserves in the ground are not reserves in storage.
group.note: The 290 million-barrel stock is measured; the speed and legal basis of Venezuelan replenishment remain unspecified.

background.title: The programme tries to solve two depleted systems with one agreement
background.text: The United States wants to rebuild an emergency stockpile reduced by more than 100 million barrels this year while also lowering exposure to disrupted Middle Eastern supply. Venezuela wants capital and operating capacity after years of underinvestment and sanctions. Those aims can align, but only through a long chain: legal title, licences, field rehabilitation, diluent and power supply, export terminals, shipping, purchase terms and storage compatibility. Caracas describes a 25-year development programme and 1.5 million-barrel-per-day target; U.S. officials have described broader rights. Until documents reconcile those accounts, the safest reading is a strategic framework with unresolved execution.
background.known: The U.S. reserve level and presidential statement are public; both governments acknowledge an oil agreement.
background.new: Trump explicitly assigned future Venezuelan crude to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and said replenishment would begin soon.

left.label: Measured need
left.text: The SPR stood near 290 million barrels, around a 44-year low.

right.label: Unmeasured supply
right.text: No cargo volume, start date, operator, price or contract text has been published.

sources.label: Reuters · Venezuelan oil and SPR plan
AP · what is known about the wider deal

stories.title: Malaysia paired fuel relief with a national AI-access programme for young adults.
stories.changed: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim restored the monthly citizen quota for subsidised RON95 petrol from 200 to 300 litres after the Iran war lifted energy costs, raised eligible diesel quotas to 400 litres, and announced more funding for schools, digital health and small-business finance. From 1 September, Malaysians aged 18 to 30 will also receive access to selected AI products including Google's Gemini Enterprise and Alibaba Cloud tools. The e-invoicing exemption threshold for companies rises to 3 million ringgit.
stories.matters: The package treats a cost-of-living shock, small-business compliance and AI diffusion as one political problem: whether headline growth reaches households. Malaysia grew 6% in the second quarter, yet Anwar's coalition has lost three regional elections. The AI element is unusually concrete because it subsidises access rather than announcing a strategy; its value will depend on training, actual usage and whether local firms can turn tools into productivity.
stories.watch: The fiscal cost and targeting of higher fuel quotas; uptake and training for the AI programme; privacy and procurement terms; participating applications and usage limits; small-business response to the e-invoicing threshold; inflation; and whether the coalition's support improves before a possible early election.

group.label: Technology & consumer
group.title: Growth policy moved from infrastructure to household access.
group.note: The benefits are announced and dated; their fiscal cost, eligibility mechanics and productivity effect are not yet published.

background.title: A digital programme is being used as visible economic redistribution
background.text: Malaysia has strong data-centre and cloud ambitions, but national AI advantage does not automatically reach students, workers or small firms. Free product access lowers one barrier while the fuel and microfinance measures address immediate household pressure. Combining them is politically legible: the government can say growth funds both today's consumption and tomorrow's capability. The risk is that subsidised licences become unused entitlements if devices, connectivity, training and work processes do not change. The programme is therefore an adoption experiment, not evidence of productivity gains.
background.known: The prime minister announced the quotas, funding, age range, named tools, e-invoicing threshold and 1 September start.
background.new: Malaysia connected emergency cost relief with broad access to enterprise AI products in a single national package.

left.label: Immediate benefit
left.text: Fuel quotas rise and compliance relief begins from 1 September.

right.label: Outcome unproved
right.text: No usage targets, fiscal cost or productivity measurement has been released.

stories.title: Qatar's Himyan cards can now be added to Samsung Wallet.
stories.changed: Qatar Central Bank and Samsung Gulf integrated eligible Himyan debit and prepaid cards into Samsung Wallet for compatible Galaxy phones and watches. Payments use device tokenisation, Samsung Knox and biometric or PIN authentication at contactless terminals. Cardholders add a card through the wallet and complete verification with the issuing bank.
stories.matters: Himyan is Qatar's locally managed national payment scheme. Putting it inside a global device wallet removes a practical adoption disadvantage without surrendering the domestic payment rail itself. The move can widen usage and reduce dependence on physical cards, but its real reach depends on how many banks and cards are eligible and whether users encounter the same reliability they expect from international schemes.
stories.watch: The list of participating banks and eligible cards; Android device compatibility; transaction limits, fees and dispute handling; token provisioning failures; merchant acceptance; active-card and wallet-usage data; and whether Himyan reaches Apple Pay and Google Wallet on equivalent terms.

group.label: Qatar
group.title: A national rail gained a mainstream consumer interface.
group.note: The technical integration is live; adoption, bank coverage and transaction performance are the next evidence.

background.title: Local control only matters if the customer experience travels with it
background.text: A domestic card scheme can strengthen resilience, data governance and competition, but users compare it with the fastest global payment experiences. Wallet tokenisation lets the card remain issued on Himyan while the device stores a substitute credential rather than the card number. Samsung Knox isolates payment data and biometrics authorise the transaction. That makes the infrastructure more usable, not automatically more used. Bank enrolment, phone penetration and routine acceptance will determine whether the integration changes payment behaviour.
background.known: QCB says eligible debit and prepaid cards can now be provisioned on compatible Galaxy devices and used at contactless points of sale.
background.new: Himyan has moved from physical-card infrastructure into Samsung's consumer wallet.

left.label: Live capability
left.text: Eligible Himyan cards can be tokenised after issuer verification.

right.label: Reach undisclosed
right.text: QCB did not publish participating-bank coverage or adoption targets.

stories.title: Guinea-Bissau voted on a constitution that would concentrate power before its return to elections.
stories.changed: Voters went to the polls under military rule on a constitution that would let the president appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet, dissolve parliament in a grave crisis and reshape ministries. It would also reduce parliament from 102 seats to 65. Reporters observed low turnout after major opposition groups called for a boycott. Counting began overnight; no reliable national result was available at publication time.
stories.matters: The referendum is presented as the bridge from last November's coup to December elections, but it also rewrites the rules in favour of the office the transition is meant to fill. A low-turnout approval could give the process formal legitimacy without resolving opposition claims that the military designed the constitution to entrench executive control. The country is a test of whether a scheduled election actually restores checks after a coup.
stories.watch: Official turnout and vote share; independent observation; Supreme Court validation; candidate eligibility rules; whether the transitional leader runs; opposition participation in December; the treatment of disputed 2025 results; and the response from ECOWAS and the African Union.

group.label: Governance
group.title: The transition wrote stronger presidential power into its exit route.
group.note: The constitutional text and boycott are established; the result and legitimacy of turnout remain open.

background.title: Institutional design is the substance, not the ceremony
background.text: Guinea-Bissau's semi-presidential system has repeatedly produced conflict between presidents and prime ministers. The military says clearer hierarchy will reduce instability. Opponents argue that the new text subordinates the cabinet, parliament and parties while shrinking representation and changing candidacy rules. The referendum follows a coup staged before authorities announced the result of a disputed presidential election. In that sequence, voting alone cannot establish a democratic transition; the decisive questions are whether power can be contested, whether the rules are neutral and whether losers retain legal protection.
background.known: The published draft expands presidential authority, cuts parliamentary seats and precedes December elections; opposition parties urged a boycott.
background.new: Voting took place with visibly low participation, moving the contest from constitutional drafting to turnout and acceptance.

left.label: Formal transition step
left.text: A referendum and December election calendar exist.

right.label: Legitimacy unresolved
right.text: The result, turnout and opposition acceptance were not established by publication time.

sources.label: AP · vote, boycott and constitutional stakes
Reuters · powers in the proposed constitution

stories.sourceNote: Niger state television + AP · Sunday update
stories.title: Niamey returned to calm after Russian-backed forces suppressed the mutiny.
stories.changed: Niger's capital appeared calm on Sunday after loyalist units, supported by Russian troops, repelled soldiers who had attacked the airport air base and the presidential district. Authorities arrested or killed dozens of mutineers and displayed some detainees on state television. The government did not publish charges, a unit-by-unit account or a full casualty tally.
stories.matters: The update confirms survival, not restored cohesion. Niger expelled Western security partners and tied its counterterrorism strategy to Russia after the 2023 coup. Needing Russian help to defend the capital from its own soldiers exposes the depth of that dependency, while arrests and purges may divert forces from the jihadist violence that helped produce military anger.
stories.watch: A public appearance and command statement from junta leader Abdourahamane Tchiani; the identity and home units of detainees; military purges; Russian Africa Corps deployments; airport operations; reprisals; and whether jihadist groups exploit forces being reassigned to regime security.

group.label: Africa
group.title: The regime held the capital, but outsourced part of its survival.
group.note: Calm and arrests are visible; the military's internal fracture and Russia's exact operational role remain incompletely disclosed.

background.title: Regime security and national security have separated
background.text: The officers who seized power promised better protection from jihadist groups and closer sovereignty after ending Western military partnerships. Violence instead intensified, and soldiers from heavily affected regions were reported among the mutineers. The airport base is both an air-force site and headquarters for the Niger–Mali–Burkina Faso force, so losing it even temporarily was more than a symbolic breach. Russian assistance restored the regime's position, but it cannot by itself repair the bargain between battlefield units and the command.
background.known: Fighting subsided, loyalists retook key sites, detainees were shown publicly and multiple accounts attribute assistance to Russian forces.
background.new: The immediate control question shifted toward the longer question of purges, cohesion and foreign dependence.

left.label: Control restored
left.text: Normal activity returned and the airport and presidency remained with loyalists.

right.label: Cohesion not restored
right.text: The government has not explained the mutiny's scale, grievances or command penetration.

sources.label: AP · inside the mutiny and Russian intervention

radar.label: Qatar telecoms
radar.title: Vodafone Qatar separated its tower assets into a wholly owned infrastructure subsidiary.
radar.text: Infinity Signal Services will manage passive assets and future network growth. The corporate structure is confirmed; financing, tenancy model and any eventual asset monetisation are not.

radar.label: Qatar tourism
radar.title: A weekly Armenia–Doha leisure charter is expected to bring about 6,500 visitors through May.
radar.text: The first charter after the regional disruption is a useful restoration signal, but it is one contracted source market—not yet evidence of a broad tourism recovery.

radar.label: Ukraine
radar.title: The Kyiv-area ammunition-depot death toll rose to 38, with four people missing.
radar.text: The national storage audit remains the consequential follow-up. A one-person toll revision does not change yesterday's diagnosis of a logistics failure multiplied by a Russian strike.

radar.label: Currencies
radar.title: The yen slipped back through 160 while Washington called the move contained.
radar.text: Bessent's language reduces the near-term signal for another joint intervention. Watch disorderly speed, not the threshold alone.

attention.title: Reuters' account of the renewed U.S.–Iran exchange
attention.text: It is the cleanest starting point for what is confirmed: the Larak targets, the timing after a month-long pause, the attributed Iranian response and the immediate limit of damage reporting.

ignore.title: Claims that China's economy has already rebounded
ignore.text: Manufacturing nearly stabilised, but services, construction, employment, smaller firms and the composite index remained in contraction. One better headline is not broad recovery.

history.title: India's Green Revolution was not a miracle seed. It was a machine built around one.
history.deck: Semi-dwarf wheat is often credited with rescuing South Asia from famine. The plant mattered enormously, but seed alone could not make harvests jump. Mexico's breeding programme, Indian scientists, emergency imports, irrigation, fertiliser, credit, guaranteed prices, procurement and storage had to lock together. The result created food security—and a set of environmental and political obligations that India still carries.
history.thesis: A breakthrough becomes history only when institutions build the complementary system that lets ordinary people use it at scale; that same system also fixes new incentives and costs into place.

sections.title: The problem was not simply that wheat yielded too little
sections.text: In the 1940s, Mexico invited the Rockefeller Foundation to help raise farm output after years of low productivity and disease. Norman Borlaug joined a programme breeding wheat against stem rust, a fungus capable of destroying a crop across large areas. He and Mexican colleagues planted in different seasons and locations, compressing breeding cycles and exposing candidate plants to varied conditions. Moving seed between Mexico's central plateau and the northern Yaqui Valley allowed two generations in a year and selected plants that were less sensitive to day length. The programme produced disease-resistant lines, but higher yield created another problem: traditional tall wheat fell over when fertiliser made the grain head heavier. The biological bottleneck was architecture as much as disease. A plant had to remain standing while converting more water and nitrogen into grain.

sections.title: Semi-dwarf wheat made high inputs productive
sections.text: Crosses with Japanese dwarfing genes produced shorter, stronger stems that resisted lodging and directed a larger share of growth into the grain. The new varieties were not magical in every field. Their advantage appeared when water arrived reliably, fertiliser supplied nutrients, weeds and pests were managed, and farmers planted at the right time. Mexico's achievement was therefore a package: genetics multiplied the return on irrigation and fertiliser, while extension, farmer training and seed multiplication carried the package beyond experiment stations. The varieties also had to keep resisting evolving rust pathogens, so breeding remained a continuing service rather than a one-time invention. By the late 1950s Mexico had become self-sufficient in wheat, and its research network became the institutional ancestor of CIMMYT.

sections.title: India adopted the package under political pressure
sections.text: India entered the mid-1960s with rapid population growth, drought, thin grain reserves and heavy dependence on food imports. The memory of the Bengal famine and the humiliation of living 'ship to mouth' made self-sufficiency a security objective, not only an agricultural one. Indian geneticist M. S. Swaminathan helped bring Borlaug and the Mexican lines into the national research system, where breeders could test, cross and adapt them rather than merely copy an imported product. In 1966 India imported an unprecedented quantity of seed and concentrated the first push in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, where irrigation and administrative capacity already existed. The strategy deliberately started where success was most likely rather than distributing scarce inputs evenly. That choice accelerated results, but it also set the geography of later advantage.

sections.title: The state built a market that made experimentation rational
sections.text: Farmers would not replace familiar seed merely because scientists promised higher potential. The new crop required cash for fertiliser, pumps and equipment and exposed growers to price risk if everyone harvested more grain at once. India created complementary institutions: coordinated research and extension, rural credit, fertiliser supply, irrigation works, minimum support prices, the Agricultural Prices Commission and the Food Corporation of India. Public procurement guaranteed a buyer, storage carried grain across seasons and the distribution system moved it toward consumers. Procurement also created information: an announced floor price told farmers before planting that the state intended to absorb part of the surplus. The state did not just spread technology; it made adoption financeable and protected the new abundance from collapsing its own incentive.

sections.title: The harvest transformed the country's bargaining position
sections.text: Wheat output accelerated sharply after the 1965–67 droughts, and record crops replaced chronic emergency imports with national stocks. Production gains later extended through high-yielding rice. The change reduced famine risk, lowered real wheat prices over time and gave New Delhi more freedom from foreign food aid. CIMMYT's historical assessment estimates that the price Indian consumers paid for wheat fell by about 2% a year from 1970 to 1995, spreading part of the productivity gain far beyond farms. Domestic abundance also let the public distribution system expand into poorer and more remote areas. The visible hero was a short plant, but the strategic result came from a chain that began with international research and ended with Indian procurement, warehouses and ration shops. Remove enough links and the same seed would have remained a promising trial.

sections.title: The machine solved scarcity by concentrating resources
sections.text: The package rewarded regions with canals, groundwater, roads and procurement access, widening advantages over rain-fed areas. Cheap power encouraged tube wells; guaranteed purchases favoured wheat and rice; fertiliser subsidies and simplified rotations increased pressure on soil and water. Groundwater depletion, salinity, nutrient imbalance, pesticide damage and crop homogeneity are not proof that the original food-security achievement was false. They are evidence that a system optimised for one emergency continued after its constraints changed. Farmers rationally followed prices and infrastructure built for maximum grain; changing outcomes therefore requires changing the surrounding system, not blaming individuals for using it. The next agricultural transition must preserve dependable yields while redesigning incentives around water, soil, diversity and climate resilience. The lesson is neither worship nor rejection of technology: complementarity creates power, and path dependence creates the bill.

timeline.text: Mexico and the Rockefeller Foundation begin the agricultural programme that will develop disease-resistant, high-yield wheat.
Mexico reaches wheat self-sufficiency after breeding, irrigation and farm practices reinforce one another.
Norman Borlaug visits India; M. S. Swaminathan and Indian institutions test the Mexican semi-dwarf lines.
India establishes the Agricultural Prices Commission and Food Corporation to support prices, procurement and storage.
India launches the high-yielding varieties programme and imports seed at unprecedented scale amid drought and food insecurity.
Borlaug receives the Nobel Peace Prize as wheat output surges across India and Pakistan.
